title: Physical properties of matter
competency: Describe physical properties and use them to identify substances.

keywords.def: A property we can measure or observe without changing what the substance is.
A property that depends on the amount of sample: length, mass, volume.
A property that does not depend on the amount: density, colour, melting point, hardness.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid. Ice: 0 °C.
The temperature at which a liquid boils. Water at sea level: 100 °C.
Mass per unit volume: d = m/V, in kg/m³.
The ability of a substance to conduct electricity.

en.text: A physical property can be measured or observed without changing what the substance is. Colour, odour, taste, state, melting point, boiling point, density and conductivity are physical properties. Melting ice is still water, so melting point is a physical property.

screens.title: Still water?
screens.ask: You measure the temperature at which ice melts. Is the water still water afterwards?
opts: No, it becomes a new substance
screens.after: It is still water. Measuring the melting point did not change what it is. That is a physical property.

screens.title: 2.2.1 Physical properties of matter
paras: Substances are identified by their properties.
A physical property can be measured and observed without changing the composition.
Melting ice gives water. Water differs from ice only in appearance.
We can freeze the water to get ice back.
So melting point is a physical property.

screens.title: Physical properties detected by sense organs
table: Chalk is white, water is colourless, gold is yellow
Water is odourless, flowers are fragrant, orange is fruity
Honey is sweet, lemon is sour, table salt is salty
screens.note: Caution! Smell and taste only safe substances. Never taste anything in the laboratory.

screens.title: Physical state
paras: Physical state is the form of a substance at a given temperature and pressure.
Water is solid below 0 °C, liquid between 0 °C and 100 °C, and gas above 100 °C.

screens.title: Water: solid, liquid or gas?
screens.ask: Tap each temperature range (at sea level).

screens.title: Key words
defs: A property we can measure or observe without changing what the substance is.

screens.text: Physical property: which one is a physical property?
screens.why:
A physical property is observed without changing the substance.
Looking at copper's colour leaves it copper.
Rusting, burning and spoiling make new substances.
So the colour of copper is the physical property.
screens.clue: Which one leaves the substance the same?

screens.why:
Colour: we see it with our eyes (light).
Odour: we smell it with our nose.
Taste: we taste it with our tongue.
screens.text: Match each physical property to the sense organ that detects it.

screens.ask: Taste is a physical property: honey is sweet, table salt is salty and lemon is ___.
screens.why:
Taste is detected by the tongue.
Honey is sweet; table salt is salty.
Lemon juice is acidic: it tastes sour.
Answer: sour.

screens.text: Safety: you may taste lemon at home but never an acid in the laboratory. Why?
opts: Laboratory acids may be strong and harmful
screens.ans: Laboratory acids may be strong and harmful
screens.why:
Lemon juice is a weak acid that is safe in food.
Laboratory acids may be strong, harmful or dirty.
They can burn the mouth or poison you.
So tasting is only for safe substances, never in the laboratory.

screens.text: Physical state of water: at what temperatures is water a liquid (at sea level)?
screens.why:
Ice melts (and water freezes) at 0 °C.
Water boils at 100 °C at sea level.
Below 0 °C it is solid ice; above 100 °C it is a gas.
So it is a liquid between 0 °C and 100 °C.
screens.clue: Use the melting point and the boiling point.

en.text: Extensive properties depend on how much sample you have: length, mass, volume. Intensive properties do not: density, colour, melting point, hardness. Intensive properties help us tell substances apart, because they do not change from sample to sample.

screens.title: Cup or bucket
screens.ask: A cup of water and a bucket of water. Which is the same for both?
screens.after: Both boil at 100 °C. Mass and volume depend on how much water there is.

screens.title: Two kinds of physical property
paras: Extensive physical properties depend on the amount of sample. Examples: length, diameter, mass, volume.
Intensive physical properties do not depend on the amount. Examples: density, colour, melting point, hardness.
Intensive properties help us tell substances apart.

screens.title: More water, same boiling point
screens.note: Move the slider. Mass and volume grow with the amount. Boiling point and density stay the same.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A property that depends on the amount of sample: length, mass, volume.
A property that does not depend on the amount: density, colour, melting point, hardness.

screens.text: Intensive property: which one stays the same whatever the amount?
screens.why:
Imagine a small and a big piece of ice.
The big one has more mass, more volume and more length.
Both still melt at 0 °C.
So melting point is the intensive property.
screens.clue: Does it change if you have more?

screens.why:
Imagine twice as much sample.
Length, mass and volume double: extensive.
Boiling point, colour and density stay the same: intensive.
screens.clue: Imagine twice as much. Does it change?
screens.text: Sort each property: does it depend on the amount (extensive) or not (intensive)?
Using intensive properties: Dawit has two gold rings, a small one and a big one. Which property helps prove both are gold?
screens.why:
Mass and volume are extensive: the big ring has more of both.
Density is intensive: it is the same for any amount of pure gold.
So find each ring's density: d = m/V.
If both match the density of gold, both are gold.
screens.clue: Choose a property that does not depend on size.

en.text: Some physical properties are measured with apparatus. They have constant values under set conditions. Melting point is when a solid melts: ice at 0 °C. Boiling point: water boils at 100 °C at sea level. Density is mass per volume, d = m/V. Electrical conductivity is how well a substance carries electricity; metals conduct well.

screens.title: Measure it
screens.ask: Which tool do you need to find the melting point of ice?
screens.after: Melting point is a temperature, so we measure it with a thermometer.

screens.caption: A thermometer measures melting and boiling points.

screens.title: Measurable physical properties
paras: These can be measured with apparatus.
They have constant values under specific conditions.
table: Temperature at which a solid becomes liquid
Temperature at which a liquid boils
Water boils at 100 °C at sea level
Mass per unit volume: d = m/V (kg/m³)

screens.title: Density d = m ÷ V
screens.note: Double the mass and the volume together. The density stays the same: it is intensive.

screens.title: Apparatus for measurable properties
items: Measures temperature: the melting point and the boiling point.
Measures mass (m). We need it to find density.
Measures the volume (V) of a liquid, in ml. 1 ml = 1 cm³.

screens.title: Key words
defs: The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid. Ice: 0 °C.
The temperature at which a liquid boils. Water at sea level: 100 °C.
Mass per unit volume: d = m/V, in kg/m³.
The ability of a substance to conduct electricity.

screens.why:
The book writes density as d = m/V.
m is the mass and V is the volume.
So density is mass divided by volume: mass per unit volume.
"Mass × volume" is wrong: we divide, we do not multiply.

items: Needs a balance and a cylinder.
screens.why:
Colour (eyes), odour (nose) and taste (tongue) need no tool.
Density needs a balance and a measuring cylinder.
Melting point needs a thermometer. Conductivity needs a circuit.
So density, melting point and conductivity are measurable.
screens.text: Sort each property: detected by our sense organs, or measured with apparatus?

screens.ask: Density: a stone has a mass of 60 g and a volume of 20 cm³. Its density is ___ g/cm³.
screens.why:
Formula: d = m ÷ V.
m = 60 g and V = 20 cm³.
d = 60 ÷ 20 = 3.
Check: 3 × 20 = 60 ✓
So the density is 3 g/cm³.
screens.clue: Divide the mass by the volume.

screens.ask: Density, find the mass: a block of wood has a density of 0.5 g/cm³ and a volume of 40 cm³. Its mass is ___ g.
screens.why:
Start from d = m/V. Turn it around: m = d × V.
d = 0.5 g/cm³ and V = 40 cm³.
m = 0.5 × 40 = 20.
Check: 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5 ✓
So the mass is 20 g.
screens.clue: Turn d = m/V around: m = d × V.

items.text: Activity 2.6 Q1: which of these physical properties have constant values under specific conditions?
items.why:
Measurable properties are measured with apparatus.
Under set conditions they always give the same value.
Pure water always melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea level.
So: melting point, boiling point and density.

items.text: Activity 2.6 Q2: which can be recognized directly by our sense organs?
items.why:
Our senses detect some properties directly.
Eyes see colour, the nose smells odour, the tongue tastes.
Melting point, boiling point and density need tools.
So: odour, colour and taste.

items.text: Activity 2.6 Q4 (melting point): what will happen to ice kept in a cup in the classroom?
items.why:
Ice melts at 0 °C.
A classroom is much warmer than 0 °C.
So the ice takes in heat and melts into water.
It is still water: only its state changes.

items.text: Activity 2.6 Q6 (taste): how do you describe the taste of lemon?
items.why:
Taste is sensed by the tongue.
Lemon juice is acidic.
Acidic foods taste sour.
Answer: sour.

items.text: Activity 2.7 (safety): why are you never allowed to taste any acid in the laboratory?
opts: Laboratory acids may be strong, harmful or contaminated
items.ans: Laboratory acids may be strong, harmful or contaminated
items.why:
Laboratory acids can be strong and burn the mouth and throat.
They may also be harmful or contaminated (dirty).
Tasting is used only when a substance is known to be safe.
So never taste anything in the laboratory.

test.text: Physical or chemical: which one is a physical property?
test.why:
Measuring a melting point does not change the substance.
Flammability, rusting and reactivity are about forming new substances.
Those three are chemical properties.
Answer: melting point.

test.ask: Boiling point: pure water boils at ___ °C at sea level.
test.why:
The boiling point of pure water at sea level is 100 °C.
It is a measurable property with a constant value.
Answer: 100.

test.text: Extensive property: which one depends on the amount of sample?
test.why:
Imagine twice as much sample.
Colour, density and melting point stay the same.
Mass doubles.
So mass is the extensive property.

test.text: Physical properties (Review Exercise): the interaction of a substance with light results in its …
test.why:
Light falls on a substance.
Some light is taken in; some bounces back to our eyes.
What we see is the colour of the substance.
Answer: colour.

test.ask: Density: an object has a mass of 50 g and a volume of 10 cm³. Its density is ___ g/cm³.
test.why:
Formula: d = m ÷ V.
d = 50 ÷ 10 = 5.
Check: 5 × 10 = 50 ✓
So the density is 5 g/cm³.
